# Data and plans

```{r setup}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(duckknit)

options(
  duckdb.home = "~/.duckdb",
  width = 80,
  pillar.print_max = 6,
  pillar.print_min = 6
)

# dbplyr's default header prints the absolute path of the database file, which is wider than a slide
loadNamespace("dbplyr"); loadNamespace("duckdb")
registerS3method("db_connection_describe", "duckdb_connection", function(con) {
  paste0("DuckDB [", basename(DBI::dbGetInfo(con)$dbname), "]")
}, envir = asNamespace("dbplyr"))

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.align = "center", fig.retina = 2, dpi = 150,
  out.width = "100%"
)

# duckknit chunks are labelled as SQL so they are highlighted, styled, and copyable
knitr::opts_hooks$set(engine = function(options) {
  if (options$engine == "duckdb") {
    options$lang = "sql"
    options$class.source = "duckdb-cli"
    options$prompt = TRUE
  }
  options
})

# Python must be initialized while the working directory still holds .venv
reticulate::use_virtualenv(normalizePath(".venv"), required = TRUE)

# Taxi data and derived files live outside the repo; use that directory by default
data_dir = path.expand("~/Scratch/duckdb")
stopifnot(dir.exists(data_dir))
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = data_dir)
```

```{r setup_data}
#| include: false
# Derived files that the deck reads but does not create on every render
con = DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
if (!file.exists("tpch.duckdb")) {
  DBI::dbExecute(con, "INSTALL tpch; LOAD tpch; CALL dbgen(sf = 1)")
  DBI::dbExecute(con, "ATTACH 'tpch.duckdb' AS tpch")
  DBI::dbExecute(con, "COPY FROM DATABASE memory TO tpch")
  DBI::dbExecute(con, "DETACH tpch")
}
if (!file.exists("yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet")) {
  file.copy("~/Scratch/nyc-taxi/yellow/yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet", ".")
}
derived = c(
  "yellow_tripdata_2026-09.csv" = "COPY taxi TO 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09.csv'",
  "yellow_tripdata_2026-09_uncompressed.parquet" = "COPY taxi TO 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09_uncompressed.parquet' (COMPRESSION uncompressed)",
  "yellow_tripdata_2026-09_snappy.parquet" = "COPY taxi TO 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09_snappy.parquet' (COMPRESSION snappy)",
  "yellow_tripdata_2026-09.duckdb" = "ATTACH 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09.duckdb' AS t; CREATE TABLE t.taxi AS FROM taxi; DETACH t"
)
missing = derived[!file.exists(names(derived))]
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  DBI::dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE taxi AS FROM 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet'")
  for (stmt in missing) DBI::dbExecute(con, stmt)
}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

invisible(duckplyr::fallback_sitrep())
unlink("yellow_tripdata_sorted.parquet")

s = duckknit::duckknit_start_session("pq")
duckknit::duckknit_exec(s, paste0(".cd ", data_dir))
duckknit::duckknit_exec(s, ".maxrows 6")
duckknit::duckknit_exec(s, ".maxwidth 80")
duckknit::duckknit_exec(s, "SET disabled_optimizers = 'compressed_materialization';")
```

## EXPLAIN {.scrollable}

Prefixing a query with `EXPLAIN` returns the plan DuckDB will run rather than the result. The plan is a tree of operations, read from the bottom up.

::: {.mxsmall}
```{duckdb}
EXPLAIN
SELECT payment_type, count(*) AS n
FROM 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet'
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY n DESC;
```
:::

::: {.aside}
`EXPLAIN` is not part of ANSI SQL but is widely supported - what it returns and how it is read varies widely between engines.
:::

## Reading a plan

The following are some of the steps you will see in DuckDB's plans:

::: {.small}
| Operator                       | Description                                                        |
|--------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `* Scan`                     | Read a table or file, e.g. `Table Scan`, `Parquet Scan`            |
| `Filter`                       | Apply a `WHERE` condition                                          |
| `Projection`                   | Compute and select output columns (`SELECT`)                       |
| `Hash Join`                    | Join by building a hash table on one input and probing with the other |
| `Hash Group By`                | Group rows and compute aggregates with a hash table (`GROUP BY`)   |
| `Ungrouped Aggregate`          | A single aggregate over all rows                                   |
| `Order By`                     | Sort rows                                                          |
| `Top N`                        | `ORDER BY` with a `LIMIT`, keeps only the needed rows              |
:::

Each box also lists the columns it needs (`Projections`), any filters it applies, and the estimated number of rows, which is what the optimizer uses to choose between plans. Estimates come from statistics such as a column's range or a file's row count, so they can be far from the actual counts.


## EXPLAIN ANALYZE {.scrollable}

Adding the `ANALYZE` keyword runs the query and records the number of rows and time per operation.

::: {.mxsmall}
```{duckdb}
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT payment_type, count(*) AS n
FROM 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet'
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY n DESC;
```
:::


## Aside - No indexes

Unlike most databases, DuckDB rarely uses an index. In SQLite, the trip count by `payment_type` sorts rows into a temporary B-tree to group them.

::: {.xsmall .pt-2}
```
|--SCAN taxi USING COVERING INDEX taxi_payment
`--USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY
```
:::

::: {.pt-1}
* An index pays off when a query needs a few rows. Analytical queries read much of the table, where one scan beats many lookups.
* Compressed columns and vectorized execution make scans cheap, and zone maps let a scan skip row groups.
* Pre-built indexes must be planned in advance, take space, and slow every write.
:::

::: {.aside}
DuckDB builds ART indexes for `PRIMARY KEY` and `UNIQUE` constraints or with `CREATE INDEX`. They enforce constraints and speed up very selective lookups.
:::


# Parquet Details

## Row vs column storage

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width='50%'}
Row oriented (CSV, most databases)

::: {.xsmall}
```
name,  salary, dept
Alice, 52000,  Accounting
Bob,   40000,  Accounting
Carol, 30000,  Sales
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width='50%'}
Column oriented (Parquet, DuckDB)

::: {.xsmall}
```
name:   [Alice, Bob, Carol, ...]
salary: [52000, 40000, 30000, ...]
dept:   [Accounting, Accounting, Sales]
```
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width='50%'}
Reading one column still passes over every other field in each row. Values of mixed types side by side compress poorly.
:::

::: {.column width='50%'}
Reading one column skips the others entirely. Values of one type side by side compress well.
:::
::::

Analytical queries touch a few columns of many rows, which is exactly the access pattern column storage is good at. Parquet is the standard columnar file format, used by Spark, Arrow, `pandas`, `polars`, DuckDB, and most cloud warehouses.


## Inside a Parquet file

::: {.medium}
A Parquet file is split by rows first, then by columns. 

The rows are divided into row groups. Each row group then holds one column chunk per column, with that column's values for those rows, encoded and compressed in pages.

The footer holds the schema plus, for every column chunk, its location, size, and optional statistics (minimum, maximum, and null count).
:::

::: {.medium}
| Structure         | What a reader can do with it                                  |
|-------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| column chunks     | read only the columns the query needs (projection pushdown)   |
| row group stats   | skip row groups whose min / max cannot match a filter         |
| typed values      | load numbers and dates in their binary form, without converting text |
| encodings         | store repeated values once (dictionary) or as runs (run length) |
| footer            | learn the schema and plan without reading the data            |
:::

::: {.aside}
See the [Parquet format](https://parquet.apache.org/docs/file-format/) docs and DuckDB's [Parquet overview](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/data/parquet/overview).
:::


## File metadata

DuckDB exposes the footer through table functions. Our file has four large row groups of about a million rows each, with statistics recorded for every column chunk.

::: {.mxsmall}
```{duckdb}
SELECT num_rows, num_row_groups, format_version, file_size_bytes
FROM parquet_file_metadata('yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet');
```
:::

. . .

```{duckdb}
#| include: false
.maxwidth 104
```

::: {.mxsmall}
```{duckdb}
SELECT path_in_schema, row_group_id AS rg, row_group_num_rows AS n,
       stats_min, stats_max
FROM parquet_metadata('yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet')
WHERE path_in_schema = 'tpep_pickup_datetime';
```
:::

```{duckdb}
#| include: false
.maxwidth 80
```


## Counting from metadata

The Parquet footer already records the row count. DuckDB can answer this unfiltered `count(*)` without reading the data columns, just as it did in Lec17.

::: {.xsmall}
```{duckdb}
SELECT count(*) AS n
FROM 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet';
```
:::

:::: {.columns .xsmall}
::: {.column width='50%'}
```{duckdb}
EXPLAIN
SELECT count(*) AS n
FROM 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet';
```
:::

::: {.column width='50%'}
```{duckdb}
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT count(*) AS n
FROM 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet';
```
:::
::::


## Projection pushdown {.scrollable}

The scan reads only the columns a query refers to, and the summary box reports how much of the file that was.

:::: {.columns .mxsmall}
::: {.column width='50%'}
```{duckdb}
#| output-location: fragment
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT sum(trip_distance)
FROM 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet';
```
:::

::: {.column width='50%' .fragment}
```{duckdb}
#| output-location: fragment
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT sum(trip_distance), sum(total_amount),
       sum(tip_amount)
FROM 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet';
```
:::
::::


## Filter pushdown and zone maps {.scrollable}

Filter pushdown applies a condition inside the scan, so only matching rows reach later operators. Row-group pruning uses the footer's min / max statistics, which DuckDB calls zone maps, to skip groups that cannot contain a match. Pushdown can help even when no groups can be skipped.

::: {.mxsmall}
```{duckdb}
#| output-location: fragment
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT count(*)
FROM 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet'
WHERE tpep_pickup_datetime >= '2026-09-25';
```
:::



## Sorting the file {.scrollable}

Rewriting the file with DuckDB sorted by pickup time changes the row group size, from four groups of about a million rows to 32 of \~120,000, and makes each of those smaller groups cover a narrow range of times.

::: {.aside}
Sorting and rewriting takes time up front. It pays off when later queries repeatedly filter on the sorted columns - this is directly analogous to building an index in other databases.
:::

```{duckdb}
#| include: false
.maxwidth 104
```

::: {.mxsmall}
```{duckdb}
COPY (FROM 'yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet' ORDER BY tpep_pickup_datetime)
  TO 'yellow_tripdata_sorted.parquet';
```

```{duckdb}
SELECT path_in_schema, row_group_id, stats_min, stats_max
FROM parquet_metadata('yellow_tripdata_sorted.parquet')
WHERE path_in_schema = 'tpep_pickup_datetime';
```
:::

```{duckdb}
#| include: false
.maxwidth 80
```


## Sort order matters {.scrollable}

With the rows in time order, the same filter skips every row group it cannot match.

::: {.mxsmall}
```{duckdb}
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT count(*)
FROM 'yellow_tripdata_sorted.parquet'
WHERE tpep_pickup_datetime >= '2026-09-25';
```
:::

::: {.aside}
A filter on `PULocationID` still reads every row group of this file, since sorting by time scatters each location across the whole file. Sort by the columns you filter on.
:::


## Skipping whole files {.scrollable}

Recall the BTS flight data has one Parquet file per year, in folders with names like `Year=2024` (we called this Hive partitioning). DuckDB reads `Year` from the folder name and uses a filter on it to skip other years' files.

```{r}
#| include: false
flights_dir = path.expand("~/Scratch/bts_ontime")
s_flights = duckknit::duckknit_start_session("flights")
duckknit::duckknit_exec(s_flights, paste0(".cd ", flights_dir))
duckknit::duckknit_exec(s_flights, ".maxwidth 80")
duckknit::duckknit_exec(s_flights, "SET disabled_optimizers = 'compressed_materialization';")
```

::: {.mxsmall}
```{duckdb, session='flights'}
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT avg(DepDelay) AS delay
FROM 'Year=*/*.parquet'
WHERE Year = 2024;
```
:::

::: {.aside}
`Scanning Files: 1/38` shows partition pruning: whole files are skipped. Row-group pruning can skip groups within the remaining files. This query runs from the flight-data folder used in Lec17 (`/data/rdu/` on the department servers).
:::

## Compression

Part of the story is also the size of the files on disk (or memory),

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| echo: false
files = c(
  "CSV" = "yellow_tripdata_2026-09.csv",
  "Parquet, uncompressed" = "yellow_tripdata_2026-09_uncompressed.parquet",
  "DuckDB database" = "yellow_tripdata_2026-09.duckdb",
  "Parquet, Snappy" = "yellow_tripdata_2026-09_snappy.parquet",
  "Parquet, `zstd`" = "yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet"
)
sizes = fs::file_size(files)
tibble::tibble(
  Format = names(files),
  File = paste0("`", files, "`"),
  Size = format(sizes)
) |>
  arrange(desc(sizes)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "llr")
```
:::

::: {.aside}
Snappy is DuckDB's default parquet compression scheme since every reader supports it. The original file uses `zstd`, which is smaller at the cost of slower writes.
:::


## Parquet vs DuckDB files

A DuckDB database file is laid out like a Parquet file. Each table is split into row groups of 122,880 rows, and each column within a group is stored and compressed separately with min / max statistics.

::: {.small}
|              | Parquet file                          | DuckDB file                                  |
|--------------|---------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| Holds        | One table                             | Many tables, views, and constraints          |
| Compression  | Encodings plus Snappy or `zstd`       | Lightweight encodings chosen for fast reads  |
| Changes      | Written once, rewrite to change       | `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` in transactions |
| Datasets     | Split across many files and folders   | One file                                     |
| Readers      | Nearly every data tool                | DuckDB                                       |
:::

Parquet is the better choice for sharing and archiving data. A DuckDB file suits data that you query and update repeatedly from DuckDB.


# Query plans

## TPC-H

TPC-H is a standard benchmark modeled on a wholesale business. A line item is one product entry within an order. DuckDB's `tpch` extension generates the data with `CALL dbgen(sf = 1)`.

One customer → many orders; one order → many line items.

::: {.medium}
| Table      | Rows      | Columns used here                                                                  |
|------------|-----------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `customer` | 150,000   | `c_custkey`, `c_mktsegment`                                                        |
| `orders`   | 1,500,000 | `o_orderkey`, `o_custkey`, `o_orderdate`, `o_orderpriority`, `o_totalprice`        |
| `lineitem` | 6,001,215 | `l_orderkey`, `l_shipdate`, `l_quantity`, `l_extendedprice`, `l_discount`, `l_returnflag`, `l_linestatus` |
:::

`orders` joins `customer` on `o_custkey = c_custkey`, and `lineitem` joins `orders` on `l_orderkey = o_orderkey`.

::: {.aside}
The full schema has eight tables (also `part`, `supplier`, `partsupp`, `nation`, and `region`) and lives in `tpch.duckdb`, which the session attaches behind the scenes. See the [tpch extension](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/core_extensions/tpch).
:::


## Hash joins

::: {.medium}
Checking every order against every line item would mean trillions of comparisons. A hash join reads each table once instead. Take simplified versions of the two tables,
:::

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width='50%'}
`orders`

| `o_orderkey` | `o_orderpriority` |
|--------------|-------------------|
| 10           | HIGH              |
| 20           | LOW               |
| 30           | HIGH              |
:::

::: {.column width='50%'}
`lineitem`

| `l_item` | `l_orderkey` |
|----------|--------------|
| A        | 10           |
| B        | 10           |
| C        | 20           |
| D        | 20           |
| E        | 40           |
:::
::::

::: {.small}
```sql
SELECT l_item, o_orderpriority
FROM orders JOIN lineitem ON o_orderkey = l_orderkey;
```
:::

::: {.medium}
The join builds a hash table from the smaller input, keyed on the join column, then probes it with each row of the larger input. Each probe is a direct lookup rather than a search.
:::


## Build and probe

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width='50%'}
**1. Build from orders**

Hash each order, keyed by `o_orderkey`.

| Key<br>(`o_orderkey`) | Value<br>(`o_orderpriority`) |
|-----------------------|------------------------------|
| 10                    | HIGH                         |
| 20                    | LOW                          |
| 30                    | HIGH                         |
:::

::: {.column width='50%' .fragment}
**2. Probe with line items**

Look up each line item's `l_orderkey`.

| `l_item` | `l_orderkey` | `o_orderpriority`<br>(lookup result) |
|----------|--------------|--------------------------------------|
| A        | 10           | HIGH                                 |
| B        | 10           | HIGH                                 |
| C        | 20           | LOW                                  |
| D        | 20           | LOW                                  |
| E        | 40           | no match                             |
:::
::::

::: {.medium .fragment}
This inner join produces four rows. Orders 10 and 20 each appear twice because two line items match each. Item E is dropped because no order has key 40, and order 30 is never looked up because no line item refers to it.
:::

::: {.aside}
Outer joins use the same build and probe, and differ only in what happens to unmatched rows. An unmatched line item, like E, is kept with a `NULL` priority. To keep unmatched orders, like 30, the hash table marks each entry that finds a match and emits the unmarked ones after probing ends.
:::

## A real query

How much revenue did each order priority bring in since 1998? 

. . .

```{duckdb}
#| include: false
ATTACH 'tpch.duckdb' AS tpch (READ_ONLY);
USE tpch;
.timer on
```

::: {.xsmall}
```{duckdb}
SELECT o_orderpriority, count(*) AS n,
       round(sum(l_extendedprice * (1 - l_discount))) AS revenue
FROM orders JOIN lineitem ON o_orderkey = l_orderkey
WHERE o_orderdate >= '1998-01-01'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY o_orderpriority;
```
:::

```{duckdb}
#| include: false
.timer off
```


## The join plan {.scrollable}

::: {.mxsmall}
```{duckdb}
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT o_orderpriority, count(*) AS n,
       round(sum(l_extendedprice * (1 - l_discount))) AS revenue
FROM orders JOIN lineitem ON o_orderkey = l_orderkey
WHERE o_orderdate >= '1998-01-01'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY o_orderpriority;
```
:::

## Reading the join plan

* `Table Scan` of `orders` (right) applies the date filter inside the scan and reads only `o_orderkey` and `o_orderpriority`. Its 133,623 rows form the build side.

* `Table Scan` of `lineitem` (left) reads three columns. Its `Dynamic Filters` line uses the order keys from the hash table to drop line items with no matching order, so only 535,027 of 6 million rows leave the scan.

* `Hash Join` builds a hash table from the orders, then probes it with the line items. The table must be in memory before probing starts, so the optimizer puts the smaller input on the build side, estimating about 300,000 orders against 6 million line items.

* `Hash Group By` reduces the joined rows to one row per priority. Each order can match several line items, and `n` counts the matched line items.


## Optimization

These two queries filter `orders` at different points, after the join and before it. `EXPLAIN` gives the exact same plan for both, so DuckDB runs them identically. Write the version that reads best.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Queries

:::: {.columns .xsmall}
::: {.column width='50%'}
```{duckdb}
#| eval: false
SELECT o_orderpriority, count(*) AS n
FROM orders JOIN lineitem
  ON o_orderkey = l_orderkey
WHERE o_orderdate >= '1998-01-01'
GROUP BY ALL;
```
:::

::: {.column width='50%'}
```{duckdb}
#| eval: false
SELECT o_orderpriority, count(*) AS n
FROM lineitem JOIN (
  FROM orders
  WHERE o_orderdate >= '1998-01-01'
) AS o ON l_orderkey = o_orderkey
GROUP BY ALL;
```
:::
::::

In the shared plan, the optimizer

* moved the date filter into the `orders` scan
* read only the columns each scan needs
* chose `orders`, the smaller input, as the build side
* added a dynamic filter to the `lineitem` scan, visible with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`

### Plan

::: {.xxsmall}
```{duckdb}
#| echo: false
EXPLAIN
SELECT o_orderpriority, count(*) AS n
FROM orders JOIN lineitem ON o_orderkey = l_orderkey
WHERE o_orderdate >= '1998-01-01'
GROUP BY ALL;
```
:::
:::



```{duckdb}
#| include: false
.timer off
USE memory;
DETACH tpch;
```


# `dbplyr` and `duckplyr`

## Two routes from `dplyr` to DuckDB

::: {.small}
|                      | `dbplyr`                                 | `duckplyr`                                                       |
|----------------------|------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Translates verbs to  | SQL sent to the database                 | DuckDB's relational API, no SQL                                  |
| Works with           | Any database with a backend              | DuckDB only                                                      |
| Input                | A database table, `tbl()`                | A data frame or file, `as_duckdb_tibble()`, `read_parquet_duckdb()` |
| Result               | A lazy table, `collect()` for a tibble   | A data frame, computed when needed                               |
| Unsupported function | Passed through to SQL as is              | Falls back to `dplyr` in R                                       |
| Semantics            | SQL's (`NULL`, ordering, aggregates)     | `dplyr`'s, with the same results as `dplyr`                      |
:::

`duckplyr` is the tidyverse's drop-in DuckDB backend. It promises unchanged `dplyr` code, DuckDB speed where possible, and `dplyr` behavior where not.


## `duckplyr` frames

`read_parquet_duckdb()` and `as_duckdb_tibble()` return a `duckplyr_df`. Nothing is read until a result is needed, and printing shows a preview.

::: {.xsmall}
```{r}
#| message: false
taxi = duckplyr::read_parquet_duckdb("yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet")
class(taxi)
```
:::

. . .

::: {.xsmall}
```{r}
(q = taxi |>
  filter(payment_type == 1) |>
  summarize(n = n(), .by = PULocationID) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  head(3)
)
```
:::


## The plan {.scrollable}

`explain()` on a `duckplyr` frame prints the DuckDB plan, 

::: {.mxsmall}
```{r}
explain(q)
```
:::


## Large input, small result

Our taxi summary reads millions of trips but returns only three rows.

* The input can be larger than RAM while the result fits comfortably in R or pandas.

* DuckDB can process data in chunks and spill intermediate data to temporary disk storage when needed. Spilling makes disk space and speed part of the query's resource needs.

* Collecting a large result into an ordinary R or pandas data frame still requires memory for that result. Filter and summarize in DuckDB before bringing the result into your analysis.


## Materialization

A lazy query describes work that has not yet produced a stored result. Materialization executes that work and stores the result as concrete data.

Like with `dbplyr`, `collect()` explicitly brings the result into R as a tibble:

::: {.xsmall}
```{r}
q |> collect()
```
:::

A `duckplyr` frame can also materialize automatically when an R function asks for its data. 

Prudence controls when this is allowed.


## Prudence {.wrap-output}

A `duckplyr` frame is a data frame, so any R function can ask for its rows. Whether that is allowed is controlled by its prudence,

* `lavish`, materialize whenever asked (the default for `as_duckdb_tibble()`),

* `thrifty`, materialize if the result is small (the default for `read_parquet_duckdb()`),

* `stingy`, never materialize automatically, `collect()` or `as_tibble()` must be explicit.

::: {.xsmall}
```{r}
#| error: true
nrow(taxi)
```
:::

::: {.aside}
See the [prudence](https://duckplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/prudence.html) article. Prudence protects against accidentally pulling a 10 GB Parquet file into R because a function like `nrow()` or `View()` asked for it.
:::


## Fallback {.wrap-output}

When `duckplyr` cannot translate an operation for DuckDB, it falls back to `dplyr`, silently by default. `fallback_config(info = TRUE)` reports when it happens.

::: {.xxsmall}
```{r}
duckplyr::fallback_config(info = TRUE)
taxi_lavish = duckplyr::read_parquet_duckdb("yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet", prudence = "lavish")
```

```{r fallback_slow}
#| cache: true
taxi_lavish |> filter(tpep_pickup_datetime >= as.POSIXct("2026-09-15", tz = "UTC")) |> count()
```
:::

. . .

`duckplyr` cannot translate this `as.POSIXct()` call, so the filter runs in R after materializing the file. Computing the constant first gives DuckDB a timestamp value it can compare directly:

::: {.xxsmall}
```{r}
cutoff = as.POSIXct("2026-09-15", tz = "UTC")
taxi_lavish |> filter(tpep_pickup_datetime >= cutoff) |> count()
```
:::


## Fallback and prudence {.wrap-output}

A thrifty or stingy frame refuses a fallback that would materialize too much, so the mistake surfaces as an error rather than a slow silent success.

::: {.xsmall}
```{r}
#| error: true
taxi |> filter(tpep_pickup_datetime >= as.POSIXct("2026-09-15", tz = "UTC")) |> count()
```
:::

::: {.aside}
See the [fallback](https://duckplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/fallback.html) article for what `duckplyr` can and cannot translate. `fallback_sitrep()` summarizes the fallbacks that have been logged.
:::


```{r}
#| include: false
duckplyr::fallback_config(info = FALSE)
```


## Which one

::: {.medium}
Use `dbplyr` when

* the data already lives in a database, DuckDB or otherwise, and should stay there,

* you want to see or hand edit the SQL, or need a DuckDB function with no R equivalent,

* you need to write tables, which goes through `DBI` and `compute()`.

Use `duckplyr` when

* you have `dplyr` code and data frames or Parquet files, and want it faster without rewriting,

* `dplyr` semantics matter (results must match `dplyr` exactly),

* you are happy to let fallback handle the parts DuckDB cannot.

You can also use both in one pipeline. `duckplyr::as_tbl()` turns a `duckplyr` frame into a `dbplyr` table when you need to see or edit the SQL.
:::

::: {.aside}
`library(duckplyr)` also calls `methods_overwrite()`, which makes every data frame in the session go through DuckDB. Calling functions with `duckplyr::` leaves the rest of the session alone.
:::


# Python

## The ecosystem

In Python, DuckDB works alongside `pandas` and `polars` rather than replacing them.

::: {.medium}
* `duckdb` adds SQL and a relational API (method chains that build a query lazily) over files, remote data, and data frames already in memory.

* Like `polars`, DuckDB has a lazy, optimized, multithreaded engine. The main difference is the interface, SQL first rather than expression first.

* Unlike `pandas`, DuckDB plans a whole query before running it and uses every core.

* All three exchange data through Arrow, so moving a result from one to another is usually cheap.
:::

DuckDB can query `pandas`, `polars`, and Arrow objects in place, and return results as any of them.


## Same file, three readers

```{python}
#| include: false
import time
def timeit(label, f):
  start = time.perf_counter()
  v = f()
  print(f"{label:18s} {time.perf_counter() - start:6.3f} s   {v:.3f}")
```

`timeit()` runs a function once and prints the elapsed time and the result.

::: {.mxsmall}
```{python}
f, col = "yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet", "trip_distance"
```
```{python}
timeit("pandas",          lambda: pd.read_parquet(f)[col].mean())
timeit("pandas columns",  lambda: pd.read_parquet(f, columns=[col])[col].mean())
timeit("polars lazy",     lambda: pl.scan_parquet(f).select(pl.col(col).mean()).collect().item())
timeit("duckdb",          lambda: duckdb.sql(f"SELECT avg({col}) FROM '{f}'").fetchall()[0][0])
```
:::

. . .

The engines are all fast (other than pandas). The difference is whether the reader was told, or worked out, that only one of the twenty-one columns was needed.


## Relational API

`duckdb.read_parquet()`, `duckdb.read_csv()`, and `duckdb.sql()` return a relation (a lazy description of a query). Methods add operations, nothing runs until a result is requested.

This is the same taxi summary as the earlier `duckplyr` pipeline: the three pickup locations with the most trips where `payment_type = 1`.

::: {.xsmall}
```{python}
r = (duckdb.read_parquet("yellow_tripdata_2026-09.parquet")
     .filter("payment_type = 1")
     .aggregate("PULocationID, count(*) AS n")
     .order("n DESC")
     .limit(3)); r
```
:::

::: {.aside}
Printing a relation runs it for a preview, as a `dbplyr` table does. Expressions inside the methods are SQL fragments. `r.explain()` prints the plan and `r.sql_query()` the generated SQL.
:::


## Getting results out

A relation converts to whichever library you want to continue in. It stores the query rather than its result, so each conversion runs the query again.

:::: {.columns .mxsmall}
::: {.column width='50%'}
```{python}
r.pl()
```
:::

::: {.column width='50%' .fragment}
```{python}
r.df()
```
:::
::::

:::: {.columns .mxsmall .fragment}
::: {.column width='50%'}
```{python}
r.fetchall()
```
:::

::: {.column width='50%'}
```{python}
r.write_parquet("top3.parquet")
```
:::
::::

::: {.aside}
`r.pl(lazy=True)` returns a `polars` LazyFrame instead, to keep building the query lazily in `polars`.
:::


## Replacement scans

A SQL query can refer to a Python variable by name. DuckDB looks up `pandas`, `polars`, and Arrow objects in the calling scope and scans them in place.

::: {.xsmall}
```{python}
employees = pd.DataFrame({
  "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"],
  "salary": [52000, 40000, 30000]
})
```
:::

:::: {.columns .mxsmall}
::: {.column width='50%'}
```{python}
duckdb.sql(
  "FROM employees WHERE salary > 35000"
).df()
```
:::

::: {.column width='50%' .fragment}
```{python}
print(duckdb.sql(
  "FROM employees WHERE salary > 35000"
).explain())
```
:::
::::



## Which tool

::: {.medium}
| | `pandas` | `polars` | `duckdb` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model | eager, in memory | lazy or eager, in memory | SQL, lazy, spills to disk |
| Larger than memory | no | streaming for some queries | yes |
| Parallel | no | yes | yes |
| Strengths | ecosystem, plotting, modeling inputs | expressions, speed, strict types | SQL, files and remote data, joins at scale |
| Weak spots | memory, speed, inconsistent API | smaller ecosystem | no in place mutation of frames |
:::

In practice they are used together. Read and reduce with DuckDB or `polars`, hand the small result to `pandas` for plotting or modeling.


```{r}
#| include: false
duckknit::duckknit_kill_all_sessions()
```


# Summary {visibility="uncounted"}

## Takeaways {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.medium}
* Parquet splits rows into row groups, and each row group stores every column as a separate column chunk. Projection pushdown reads only needed columns; filter pushdown applies conditions inside the scan. Row-group pruning uses min / max statistics to skip groups, and sorting by filter columns makes this more effective.

* For these aggregates, CSV requires a full scan of the text. Parquet is well suited to analytical data at rest, and a DuckDB database can be faster for data queried repeatedly.

* `EXPLAIN` shows the physical plan with estimates, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` adds actual rows and time per operator. The optimizer chooses how to execute a join, but cannot determine whether its conditions express the relationship you intended.

* `dbplyr` translates to SQL and works with any database. `duckplyr` uses DuckDB directly with `dplyr` semantics and falls back to `dplyr`, which is convenient and occasionally very slow.

* Arrow enables efficient interchange between DuckDB, `polars`, and `pandas`. Some conversions avoid copies; others allocate memory depending on the types and representations involved.
:::

# Reference {visibility="uncounted"}

## Other result formats {visibility="uncounted"}

Other result formats include `to_arrow_table()`, `fetchnumpy()` (a dict of arrays), `fetchall()` (a list of tuples), and `to_arrow_reader(batch_size)` to stream a large result in batches.

::: {.aside}
DuckDB 2.0 removed `fetchone()` from relations, `limit(1).fetchall()` replaces it.
:::


## Further afield {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.medium}
* Extensions add features to the engine, `spatial` (geometry types and GIS functions), `httpfs` and `azure` (remote storage), `json`, `iceberg` and `delta` (lakehouse table formats), and community extensions.

* `duckdb -ui` opens a notebook style interface in the browser for exploring a database.

* `ibis` is a Python dataframe API that compiles to SQL for around twenty backends, with DuckDB as the default. It plays the role `dbplyr` does in R.

* The DuckDB engine also runs in the browser (`duckdb-wasm`) and from Java, Go, Rust, Node, and Swift.
:::

::: {.aside}
See [extensions](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/core_extensions/overview) and the [DuckDB UI](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/core_extensions/ui).
:::
